fixes.explanation: Wrath is it, baker. John says the angels hold the seven final plagues, “…with which the wrath of God is completed.” (Revelation 15:1) That's why they're called final: when these seven are done, God's wrath is completed.

Harvest has a fair claim, baker, since John saw a sickle swung over the earth just before this (Revelation 14:16). Here, though, the verse says the seven final plagues are the ones “…with which the wrath of God is completed.” (Revelation 15:1) Wrath is the word that fills this blank.

True! John says they were “…holding harps from God…” (Revelation 15:2) These are the ones who conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, and they're standing beside something like a sea of glass mixed with fire. Harps in hand, ready to sing.

This one's true, friend. John says the people standing beside something like a sea of glass “…were holding harps from God…” (Revelation 15:2) They had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name. And right after the harps comes the singing.

Moses it is. Moses was Israel's leader, and the singers sing “…the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb…” (Revelation 15:3) Moses and the Israelites once sang a song to the LORD too (Exodus 15:1). Two names on one song, and John gives us both.

David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), is a fair guess with all those harps around. But John never names him here. The song is called “…the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb…” (Revelation 15:3) The other name is Moses.

Elijah, the prophet who faced Israel's king Ahab (1 Kings 18:17-18), is a big name, friend. But he isn't in this verse. John says they sang “…the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb…” (Revelation 15:3) The other name is Moses.
The singers are standing beside something like a sea of glass, so I see how that one sneaks in. But the song never says a sea obeys Him. Their reason is, “For You alone are holy.” (Revelation 15:4)

Plenty of angels in this passage, baker, but nobody sings about their sleep schedule. The song asks, “Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name?” and then gives the reason: “For You alone are holy.” (Revelation 15:4) Sleep never comes up in it.

Bowls, baker. One of the four living creatures gave the angels “…seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever.” (Revelation 15:7) Golden bowls, and every one of them full. Keep an eye on those bowls, because the angels get their orders in the next chapter.

Trumpets do play a big part earlier in Revelation (Revelation 8:6), so I understand the guess. But in this passage the creature hands over “…seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God…” (Revelation 15:7) Bowls are what get poured out in chapter 16.

Crowns are a good guess, since Revelation has elders wearing golden crowns (Revelation 4:4). Here, though, the living creature gives the angels “…seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God…” (Revelation 15:7) Bowls, not crowns.

Not yet, friend. John says, “…no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.” (Revelation 15:8) The temple is filled with smoke from the glory of God and from His power, and nobody goes in until the plagues are done.

Those folks are standing beside something like a sea of glass, holding harps and singing (Revelation 15:2-3), so they're in a very different spot. They're the ones who conquered the beast and its image. The sores go to “…those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.” (Revelation 16:2)
Dies. The sea turns to blood “…like that of the dead, and every living thing in the sea died.” (Revelation 16:3) This is a heavy one, friend. The text says every living thing.
Hiding would mean they had somewhere to go. Revelation 16:3 says the sea turned to blood “…like that of the dead, and every living thing in the sea died.” This part is heavy.

True! John hears the altar reply, “Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments.” (Revelation 16:7) The angel of the waters speaks first, then the altar answers. Two voices, and they agree about God's judgments.
That's what the text says. The men “…curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores. Yet they did not repent of their deeds.” (Revelation 16:11) I think this is a hard verse to read.

The bowl goes on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom is plunged into darkness, so I see why that came to mind. But the text never says they turn on the beast. It says they “…curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores.” (Revelation 16:11)

Yes, that's the reason given, baker. The sixth angel's bowl goes on the Euphrates, “…and its water was dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the East.” (Revelation 16:12) The purpose comes in the same sentence as the drying, so no guessing needed.

Battle, baker. The spirits go out to the kings of the earth “…to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.” (Revelation 16:14) These are demonic spirits, and they perform signs as they go. Gathering the kings is their errand.

Worship is a good word, and the beast's image does get worshiped earlier in this passage (Revelation 16:2). But here the spirits go out “…to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.” (Revelation 16:14) So the blank wants battle.

True. Right after “Behold, I am coming like a thief.” the verse says, “Blessed is the one who remains awake and clothed, so that he will not go naked and let his shame be exposed.” (Revelation 16:15) The blessing goes to the one who stays awake and clothed. A blessing in the middle of all those bowls.
“It is done!” That's the loud voice from the throne in the temple. (Revelation 16:17) It comes when the seventh angel pours out his bowl into the air. Seven bowls, seven angels, and then those words.

No second round here, friend. The seventh angel pours out his bowl into the air, and the voice from the throne says, “It is done!” (Revelation 16:17) That's the last of the seven, and the voice doesn't send anyone back to pour.

The temple was opened back in Revelation 15:5, so I see where that came from. But after the seventh bowl, the voice from the throne says, “It is done!” (Revelation 16:17) The voice says nothing about opening anything.

That's what John says. He lists lightning, rumblings, thunder and “…a great earthquake the likes of which had not occurred since men were upon the earth—so mighty was the great quake.” (Revelation 16:18) Nothing like it had happened since people were on the earth.

Collapse. The great city was split into three parts, “…and the cities of the nations collapsed.” (Revelation 16:19) The quake doesn't stop at one city. The text says the cities of the nations, plural.

Rejoice is a hopeful word, friend, but this verse doesn't mention any celebrating. The text says the great city was split into three parts, “…and the cities of the nations collapsed.” (Revelation 16:19) Collapsed is what fills the blank.

Nothing about rebuilding shows up in this verse, baker. It says the great city was split into three parts, “…and the cities of the nations collapsed.” (Revelation 16:19) Collapse is the word that fits.

True. The verse says, “And God remembered Babylon the great and gave her the cup of the wine of the fury of His wrath.” (Revelation 16:19) God is the one who remembers her and gives her the cup. The cup holds the wine of the fury of His wrath.

True. The verse says, “And men cursed God for the plague of hail, because it was so horrendous.” (Revelation 16:21) Hailstones of almost a hundred pounds each rain down, and men curse God for that plague. Earlier, people also cursed His name (Revelation 16:9). It's a heavy way to end the bowls.
